Q: why is mise run test output not working properly?
Q2: what is the test failure I can't see because of the garbled output?
Q3. why is the test run so slow?
I’ll use the Superpowers workflow for systematic debugging here: first reproduce the test command behavior, then isolate the visible failure and where the time is going.

I’m going to inspect the project test task wiring before running the full command. The likely causes are either the wrapper around `go test`, terminal control output from the runner, or one very slow package hiding a normal failure.

The test task is just `go test ./...`, so the garbling is probably coming from raw `go test` package interleaving rather than a richer runner like `gotestsum`. I’m running the exact task now to reproduce the failure and timing.

content.text: The failing test is `TestGroupCommitsByDay_SortsNewestFirst` in `cmd/entire/cli`; the noisy output before it is from other tests writing CLI stderr/stdout directly. I’m checking that test and the helper it exercises so I can explain why it fails and why the run takes about a minute.

The specific failure is timezone-sensitive. The implementation groups commit timestamps by `t.Local()`, and this workspace is running with `Australia/Melbourne`, so two of the UTC fixture dates collapse into the same local day.

**Q1:** `mise` is not the real problem. [mise.toml](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/mise.toml:14) runs plain `go test ./...`, so when `cmd/entire/cli` fails, Go dumps all stdout/stderr from that whole package. Several tests/paths write directly to real output, for example [strategy/common.go](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/common.go:496) and [resume_test.go](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/cmd/entire/cli/resume_test.go:633). That output includes CLI messages, ANSI color, deprecation warnings, and parallel test noise, so the actual failure is buried.

**Q2:** The hidden failure is:

```text
--- FAIL: TestGroupCommitsByDay_SortsNewestFirst
activity_cmd_test.go:57: got 2 day groups, want 3
```

Root cause: [groupCommitsByDay](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/cmd/entire/cli/activity_cmd.go:208) groups dates with `t.Local().Format(...)`, while the test in [activity_cmd_test.go](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/cmd/entire/cli/activity_cmd_test.go:47) expects the three UTC fixture timestamps to remain three separate calendar days. In this workspace timezone, two January timestamps land on the same local date. I verified the targeted test passes under `TZ=UTC`.

**Q3:** The run is slow because `go test ./...` runs about 60 packages and does not stop when that fast test fails. In my run the dominant package was `github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli` at about 64s. The slowest measured tests there were the `runExplainCheckpoint(... generate=true ...)` tests around [explain_test.go](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/cmd/entire/cli/explain_test.go:2048), which go through summary generation/provider resolution rather than a cheap stub. Other slow packages include `strategy`, `checkpoint`, `agent/external`, and `summarize`; [summarize_test.go](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/cmd/entire/cli/summarize/summarize_test.go:722) also calls the default generator path.

For a clean view of this failure:

```bash
go test ./cmd/entire/cli -run TestGroupCommitsByDay_SortsNewestFirst -count=1
```

For structured output:

```bash
go test -json ./cmd/entire/cli -run TestGroupCommitsByDay_SortsNewestFirst -count=1
```
Q: can we fix the activity test to work regardless of the local machine's time zone?
I’ll use the TDD and verification skills for this small fix: keep the existing failing test as the regression signal, adjust only the fixture so it is timezone-stable, then rerun the targeted test.

I’m going to keep the production behavior unchanged and make the fixture express local calendar days explicitly. That avoids global `TZ` mutation in a parallel test and tests the behavior the function actually implements.

content.text: The integration suite is one large Go package, not many small packages. That matters because both raw `go test` and `gotestsum --format pkgname` print a package line only when the whole package exits, so with this suite there is naturally no progress output for a long time. I’m timing the interrupted test next to see whether it was actually the culprit or just the test that happened to be active when I hit Ctrl+C.

`TestEnableDefaultStrategy` is not intrinsically slow; run alone it passes in about 0.9s, and the package run takes about 3.2s including the one-time binary build. The “unknown” failure was just where the interrupted full suite happened to be, not proof that this test was hanging.

---
name: systematic-debugging
description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
---

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"

content.text: I have the root-cause shape now: `test:integration` is one large Go package, so the usual package-level output mode stays quiet until that package is done. I’m pulling the exact harness lines so the answer can point at the real choke points.

`test:integration` is quiet because it is one big Go package.

In [mise.toml](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/mise.toml:18), it runs:

```sh
go test -tags=integration ./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/...
```

That package has a `TestMain` that first builds a real `entire` binary before tests run: [setup_test.go](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/setup_test.go:13). Then most tests create temp git repos and invoke that binary as a subprocess through `execx.NonInteractive`: [testenv.go](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/testenv.go:148).

So the runtime is real integration work: binary build, temp repos, git commits, hooks, remotes, rewinds, session metadata, subprocess startup.

Why no output: raw `go test` without `-v` prints package output only when the package finishes or fails. `gotestsum --format pkgname` has the same issue here because there is only one package, so there are no intermediate package lines to print.

I ran it with per-test output:

```sh
gotestsum --format testname --format-icons text --hide-summary skipped -- -tags=integration ./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/...
```

That produced steady progress and finished `324` tests in about `88s`, with one local failure:

```text
TestLogin_SavesTokenAfterApproval
login_test.go:91: login command failed: exit status 1
Output:
Waiting for approval...
save auth token: save token to keyring: exit status 161
```

That failure is from the login integration test saving to the real local keyring: [login_test.go](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/login_test.go:89). The subprocess env does not inject a mock keyring backend: [login_test.go](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/login_test.go:193).

The slowest tests are mostly real checkpoint/session flows. Top examples from the run:

```text
TestShadow_MultipleCommits_SameActiveTurn            22.34s
TestSubagentAccumulation_Issue591                    20.38s
TestMultipleReadOnlySessions_NoneCondensed           19.8s
TestHookOverwrite_MidTurnWipe_NextPromptRecovers     19.41s
TestReadOnlySession_ActiveAcrossMultipleCommits      19.35s
```

So: it is not hung; it is quiet because of package-level output, and slow because it is doing real CLI/git integration work. The better `mise` command for this task should probably use `gotestsum --format testname`, not `pkgname`.

content.text: The fresh uncached integration run exposed the second issue I mentioned earlier: `TestLogin_SavesTokenAfterApproval` is using the real local keyring from a subprocess and intermittently fails with `exit status 161`. I’m going to fix that isolation problem too, otherwise the integration task is only “passing” when Go reuses cached results.

The keyring failure is an isolation gap: unit auth tests use `keyring.MockInit()`, but the integration login test runs a separate `entire` binary, so it hits the machine keyring. I’m adding a test-only file-backed auth store path for subprocess tests, then I’ll point the login integration at its temp file.

content.text:
Root cause of your timeout: `TestEnableDefaultStrategy` used plain `exec.Command(getTestBinary(), "enable")`. When run from your terminal, the child process inherited a real `/dev/tty`, decided it could prompt interactively, and waited in the fresh `entire enable` agent-selection flow. The test only fed `no\n` for telemetry, so it could hang until Go’s 10-minute timeout.

I fixed that in [setup_cmd_test.go](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/setup_cmd_test.go) by using `execx.NonInteractive`, matching the normal integration helper.

I also changed [mise.toml](/Users/alex/workspace/cli/.worktrees/1/mise.toml) so:

- `mise run test` uses `gotestsum --format pkgname`
- `mise run test:integration` uses `gotestsum --format testname`

That means integration now prints per-test progress instead of looking frozen for one huge package.

One more real issue showed up once the timeout was gone: `TestLogin_SavesTokenAfterApproval` was hitting the machine keyring from a subprocess and could fail with `exit status 161`. I added a test-only file-backed auth store via `ENTIRE_TEST_AUTH_STORE_FILE` and wired the login integration test to use it.

Verification run:

```text
go test -tags=integration ... TestEnableDefaultStrategy   PASS
go test -tags=integration ... TestLogin_SavesTokenAfterApproval PASS
gotestsum ... -tags=integration ... -count=1              DONE 324 tests in 84.631s
mise run test:integration                                 DONE 324 tests in 94.355s
mise run test                                             DONE 4951 tests, 4 skipped in 59.207s
mise run lint                                             0 issues
```

The suite is still inherently slow because it builds the CLI, creates temp git repos, spawns real CLI subprocesses, and exercises shadow/checkpoint/rewind flows. The slowest tests are still the 15-22s shadow/read-only/session cases, but now they are visible while running instead of silent.
and at least they don't hang?

Yes. The specific hang you hit is fixed.

`TestEnableDefaultStrategy` no longer inherits your terminal, so it can’t slip into an interactive prompt and wait forever. I verified the exact reproduction under a PTY with a 20s timeout, and the full integration suite completed afterward.

There’s still normal slowness: the fresh uncached integration run took about `85-95s`. But with `gotestsum --format testname`, you’ll see which test is currently running instead of staring at a blank terminal until timeout.
alright, cut a branch, and let's PR these local testing improvements

I’ll put only the testing-related changes on a new branch and leave the unrelated `.opencode/package-lock.json` and `docs/file-edit-tool-hooks.md` alone. I’ll also need either an appropriate Linear issue key for the PR title, or I’ll create the PR title without one if you want to bypass that repo convention.

name: finishing-a-development-branch
description: Use when implementation is complete, all tests pass, and you need to decide how to integrate the work - guides completion of development work by presenting structured options for merge, PR, or cleanup
---

# Finishing a Development Branch

## Overview

Guide completion of development work by presenting clear options and handling chosen workflow.

**Core principle:** Verify tests → Detect environment → Present options → Execute choice → Clean up.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."

## The Process

### Step 1: Verify Tests

**Before presenting options, verify tests pass:**

```bash
# Run project's test suite
npm test / cargo test / pytest / go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:**
```
Tests failing (<N> failures). Must fix before completing:

[Show failures]

Cannot proceed with merge/PR until tests pass.
```

Stop. Don't proceed to Step 2.

**If tests pass:** Continue to Step 2.

### Step 2: Detect Environment

**Determine workspace state before presenting options:**

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
```

This determines which menu to show and how cleanup works:

| State | Menu | Cleanup |
|-------|------|---------|
| `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON` (normal repo) | Standard 4 options | No worktree to clean up |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, named branch | Standard 4 options | Provenance-based (see Step 6) |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, detached HEAD | Reduced 3 options (no merge) | No cleanup (externally managed) |

### Step 3: Determine Base Branch

```bash
# Try common base branches
git merge-base HEAD main 2>/dev/null || git merge-base HEAD master 2>/dev/null
```

Or ask: "This branch split from main - is that correct?"

### Step 4: Present Options

**Normal repo and named-branch worktree — present exactly these 4 options:**

```
Implementation complete. What would you like to do?

1. Merge back to <base-branch> locally
2. Push and create a Pull Request
3. Keep the branch as-is (I'll handle it later)
4. Discard this work

Which option?
```

**Detached HEAD — present exactly these 3 options:**

```
Implementation complete. You're on a detached HEAD (externally managed workspace).

1. Push as new branch and create a Pull Request
2. Keep as-is (I'll handle it later)
3. Discard this work

Which option?
```

**Don't add explanation** - keep options concise.

### Step 5: Execute Choice

#### Option 1: Merge Locally

```bash
# Get main repo root for CWD safety
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"

# Merge first — verify success before removing anything
git checkout <base-branch>
git pull
git merge <feature-branch>

# Verify tests on merged result
<test command>

# Only after merge succeeds: cleanup worktree (Step 6), then delete branch
```

Then: Cleanup worktree (Step 6), then delete branch:

```bash
git branch -d <feature-branch>
```

#### Option 2: Push and Create PR

```bash
# Push branch
git push -u origin <feature-branch>

# Create PR
gh pr create --title "<title>" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<2-3 bullets of what changed>

## Test Plan
- [ ] <verification steps>
EOF
)"
```

**Do NOT clean up worktree** — user needs it alive to iterate on PR feedback.

#### Option 3: Keep As-Is

Report: "Keeping branch <name>. Worktree preserved at <path>."

**Don't cleanup worktree.**

#### Option 4: Discard

**Confirm first:**
```
This will permanently delete:
- Branch <name>
- All commits: <commit-list>
- Worktree at <path>

Type 'discard' to confirm.
```

Wait for exact confirmation.

If confirmed:
```bash
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"
```

Then: Cleanup worktree (Step 6), then force-delete branch:
```bash
git branch -D <feature-branch>
```

### Step 6: Cleanup Workspace

**Only runs for Options 1 and 4.** Options 2 and 3 always preserve the worktree.

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
WORKTREE_PATH=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
```

**If `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON`:** Normal repo, no worktree to clean up. Done.

**If worktree path is under `.worktrees/`, `worktrees/`, or `~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/`:** Superpowers created this worktree — we own cleanup.

```bash
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"
git worktree remove "$WORKTREE_PATH"
git worktree prune  # Self-healing: clean up any stale registrations
```

**Otherwise:** The host environment (harness) owns this workspace. Do NOT remove it. If your platform provides a workspace-exit tool, use it. Otherwise, leave the workspace in place.

## Quick Reference

| Option | Merge | Push | Keep Worktree | Cleanup Branch |
|--------|-------|------|---------------|----------------|
| 1. Merge locally | yes | - | - | yes |
| 2. Create PR | - | yes | yes | - |
| 3. Keep as-is | - | - | yes | - |
| 4. Discard | - | - | - | yes (force) |

## Common Mistakes

**Skipping test verification**
- **Problem:** Merge broken code, create failing PR
- **Fix:** Always verify tests before offering options

**Open-ended questions**
- **Problem:** "What should I do next?" is ambiguous
- **Fix:** Present exactly 4 structured options (or 3 for detached HEAD)

content.text:
Yeah, recent green builds support that this wasn’t introduced by our original changes. The race stack was in `review.PickAgents` / `multipicker.go`, which the PR hadn’t touched. It looks like a nondeterministic local `-race` exposure from starting huh/Bubble Tea with an already-cancelled context.

I hardened it anyway: `PickAgents` now returns `ErrPickerCancelled` before constructing the form if `ctx.Err() != nil`.

Pushed follow-up commit to the PR:

`ac3c01424 Avoid cancelled review picker race`

Verification:
- `go test -race ./cmd/entire/cli/review -count=1` passed
- `go test -tags=integration -race ./...` phase from `test:ci` passed
- `mise run test:e2e:canary` passed when run outside the sandbox, confirming my earlier canary failure was local permissioning under `~/.vogon`

PR is updated: https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1154
the integration tests run in 3 shards in the build...perhaps that saved it 🤔

Likely, yes.

Locally `test:integration` is one package, so it runs as one long package process. In CI, the integration suite is split into `test-integration (a)`, `(b)`, and `(c)`, so the wall time and failure surface are spread across three jobs. That helps with the “looks hung” problem and can also reduce the chance of hitting a long single-package timeout.

But the `TestEnableDefaultStrategy` hang was still real locally because that test inherited a TTY and could enter an interactive prompt. Sharding might avoid noticing it in CI if the CI subprocess has no TTY or `CI` suppresses prompts, but it doesn’t make the test correct for developer machines.
oh I meant the fact the race blows up, I would have expected to see it reflected sometimes in the build

Ah, got it. Yes, sharding could absolutely be why CI didn’t see the race.

The race was in `cmd/entire/cli/review`, and race detector failures are very schedule-sensitive. Splitting integration into 3 jobs does not directly shard `cmd/entire/cli/review`, but it reduces total concurrent work per process/job and changes timing/load. If CI runs core tests separately from integration, or with different package ordering/cache state, that can easily avoid the specific interleaving where Bubble Tea closes its cancelreader while the input goroutine is still calling `Fd()`.

Also, your pasted failure had several unrelated tests marked failed after the first race. That’s normal: once the race detector reports a race in the package, other tests running in that same package can be marked failed even though they didn’t cause it.

So: not surprising CI has been green. This looks like a latent race exposed by local scheduling, not a deterministic build break.

# Code Review Reception

## Overview

Code review requires technical evaluation, not emotional performance.

**Core principle:** Verify before implementing. Ask before assuming. Technical correctness over social comfort.

## The Response Pattern

```
WHEN receiving code review feedback:

1. READ: Complete feedback without reacting
2. UNDERSTAND: Restate requirement in own words (or ask)
3. VERIFY: Check against codebase reality
4. EVALUATE: Technically sound for THIS codebase?
5. RESPOND: Technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback
6. IMPLEMENT: One item at a time, test each
```

## Forbidden Responses

**NEVER:**
- "You're absolutely right!" (explicit CLAUDE.md violation)
- "Great point!" / "Excellent feedback!" (performative)
- "Let me implement that now" (before verification)

**INSTEAD:**
- Restate the technical requirement
- Ask clarifying questions
- Push back with technical reasoning if wrong
- Just start working (actions > words)

## Handling Unclear Feedback

```
IF any item is unclear:
  STOP - do not implement anything yet
  ASK for clarification on unclear items

WHY: Items may be related. Partial understanding = wrong implementation.
```

**Example:**
```
your human partner: "Fix 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.

❌ WRONG: Implement 1,2,3,6 now, ask about 4,5 later
✅ RIGHT: "I understand items 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before proceeding."
```

## Source-Specific Handling

### From your human partner
- **Trusted** - implement after understanding
- **Still ask** if scope unclear
- **No performative agreement**
- **Skip to action** or technical acknowledgment

### From External Reviewers
```
BEFORE implementing:
  1. Check: Technically correct for THIS codebase?
  2. Check: Breaks existing functionality?
  3. Check: Reason for current implementation?
  4. Check: Works on all platforms/versions?
  5. Check: Does reviewer understand full context?

IF suggestion seems wrong:
  Push back with technical reasoning

IF can't easily verify:
  Say so: "I can't verify this without [X]. Should I [investigate/ask/proceed]?"

IF conflicts with your human partner's prior decisions:
  Stop and discuss with your human partner first
```

**your human partner's rule:** "External feedback - be skeptical, but check carefully"

## YAGNI Check for "Professional" Features

```
IF reviewer suggests "implementing properly":
  grep codebase for actual usage

  IF unused: "This endpoint isn't called. Remove it (YAGNI)?"
  IF used: Then implement properly
```

**your human partner's rule:** "You and reviewer both report to me. If we don't need this feature, don't add it."

## Implementation Order

```
FOR multi-item feedback:
  1. Clarify anything unclear FIRST
  2. Then implement in this order:
     - Blocking issues (breaks, security)
     - Simple fixes (typos, imports)
     - Complex fixes (refactoring, logic)
  3. Test each fix individually
  4. Verify no regressions
```

## When To Push Back

Push back when:
- Suggestion breaks existing functionality
- Reviewer lacks full context
- Violates YAGNI (unused feature)
- Technically incorrect for this stack
- Legacy/compatibility reasons exist
- Conflicts with your human partner's architectural decisions

**How to push back:**
- Use technical reasoning, not defensiveness
- Ask specific questions
- Reference working tests/code
- Involve your human partner if architectural

**Signal if uncomfortable pushing back out loud:** "Strange things are afoot at the Circle K"

## Acknowledging Correct Feedback

When feedback IS correct:
```
✅ "Fixed. [Brief description of what changed]"
✅ "Good catch - [specific issue]. Fixed in [location]."
✅ [Just fix it and show in the code]

❌ "You're absolutely right!"
❌ "Great point!"
❌ "Thanks for catching that!"
❌ "Thanks for [anything]"
❌ ANY gratitude expression
```

**Why no thanks:** Actions speak. Just fix it. The code itself shows you heard the feedback.

**If you catch yourself about to write "Thanks":** DELETE IT. State the fix instead.

## Gracefully Correcting Your Pushback

If you pushed back and were wrong:
```
✅ "You were right - I checked [X] and it does [Y]. Implementing now."
✅ "Verified this and you're correct. My initial understanding was wrong because [reason]. Fixing."

❌ Long apology
❌ Defending why you pushed back
❌ Over-explaining
```

State the correction factually and move on.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| Performative agreement | State requirement or just act |
| Blind implementation | Verify against codebase first |
| Batch without testing | One at a time, test each |
| Assuming reviewer is right | Check if breaks things |
| Avoiding pushback | Technical correctness > comfort |
| Partial implementation | Clarify all items first |
| Can't verify, proceed anyway | State limitation, ask for direction |

## Real Examples

**Performative Agreement (Bad):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
❌ "You're absolutely right! Let me remove that..."
```

**Technical Verification (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
✅ "Checking... build target is 10.15+, this API needs 13+. Need legacy for backward compat. Current impl has wrong bundle ID - fix it or drop pre-13 support?"
```

**YAGNI (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Implement proper metrics tracking with database, date filters, CSV export"
✅ "Grepped codebase - nothing calls this endpoint. Remove it (YAGNI)? Or is there usage I'm missing?"
```

**Unclear Item (Good):**
```
your human partner: "Fix items 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.
✅ "Understand 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before implementing."
```

## GitHub Thread Replies

When replying to inline review comments on GitHub, reply in the comment thread (`gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr}/comments/{id}/replies`), not as a top-level PR comment.

## The Bottom Line

**External feedback = suggestions to evaluate, not orders to follow.**

Verify. Question. Then implement.

No performative agreement. Technical rigor always.
